text: I’ll treat the meshed oil as the closed interior cavity of the ring: the cylinder \(r<23\) mm, \(-5<z<5\) mm, minus the spinner material \(15<r<22\) mm, \(-4<z<4\) mm. This exactly joins the bore, radial clearance, and both 1 mm end gaps into one region. I will use the two planar cavity closures at \(z=\pm5\) mm as the requested separately named end patches; this is the only closed internal-oil interpretation that requires no unspecified external reservoir. I’ll build in metres and first inspect the coarse CAD volume.

The first bounds check exposed a placement mistake: `Cylinder` is centred by default, so the additional half-height translation shifted both bodies downward. I’ll correct that explicitly by using the centred primitives directly, then render a cutaway-style surface view of the resulting connected oil solid.

The corrected solid now has the requested centred bounds and exact analytic volume. I’ll inspect it visually with one quadrant clipped away so the bore, spinner exclusion, clearance, and end-gap connection are visible.

The cutaway confirms the intended single connected region. Next I’ll recreate this exact Boolean volume in Gmsh’s OpenCASCADE kernel and inspect every boundary entity by analytic surface type, area, and centre of mass before assigning any patch. This avoids coordinate-box patch guessing.

The seven faces match the analytic areas: three cylinders (\(r=15,22,23\) mm), two spinner annuli at \(z=\pm4\) mm, and two full cavity closures at \(z=\pm5\) mm. I’ll now assign patches from those measured surface identities, generate only the boundary mesh, and export one oriented STL per patch before creating any volume elements. The spinner patch intentionally combines its bore cylinder, outside cylinder, and two end annuli.

The boundary mesher ran, but my STL extractor tested the element-order field instead of the element-dimension field and therefore wrote empty files. The 0.25 mm surface size was also finer than a “coarse first” pass warrants. I’ll clear only the mesh, use 0.50 mm near the 1 mm gaps and 2.0 mm in the bore, then export again with the corrected triangle test.

The corrected pre-volume exports are nonempty and cover all four patches. The boundary discretization has two elements across each 1 mm gap at minimum, which is acceptable for this requested coarse mesh. I’ll now generate tetrahedra from that already-exported boundary mesh, write Gmsh 2.2 format for OpenFOAM conversion, and create only the minimal case metadata needed by mesh utilities.

Gmsh completed, but `gmshToFoam` reported 77,848 undefined boundary faces—nearly the entire surface mesh—so I will not accept this conversion. I’ll run `checkMesh` now to characterize the failure before deciding whether to change converter format or rebuild the volume mesh.
`checkMesh` stopped before reading the mesh because the minimal case lacked `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution`. I’ll add empty dictionaries (mesh checking does not need numerical schemes) and rerun it.
OpenFOAM 2512 validates required scheme subdictionaries even for `checkMesh`; I’ll supply the standard empty/default entries and try again.

The conversion is topologically connected and has good conventional quality, but 580 tetrahedra have two non-boundary faces and zero determinant. This confirms a mismatch between Gmsh’s HXT volume boundary and the pre-existing physical surface triangles. I’ll inspect the OpenFOAM boundary table before rebuilding with Gmsh’s standard Delaunay 3D algorithm, which is more conservative about preserving the supplied surface mesh.

The boundary file confirms all intended faces are named, so the defect is confined to HXT’s tetrahedralization rather than patch coverage. I’ll rebuild the same analytic volume with standard Delaunay tetrahedra, give the volume physical group a non-colliding ID, and reconvert. The already exported STLs remain untouched and still predate this volume mesh.

The standard Delaunay mesh optimized without ill-shaped tetrahedra and now labels the cell zone correctly as `oil`. The converter’s “undefined faces” message appears to be its normal pre-assignment stage because it subsequently maps the four physical patches; I’ll verify that with the binding full `checkMesh` result.

The same 580 cells fail after both tetrahedralizers, so the issue is not tetra quality; it is the converter collapsing coincident seam vertices on the periodic cylindrical CAD faces. I’ll inspect `gmshToFoam` options and then use a conversion path that preserves distinct Gmsh point identities or avoids periodic seam duplication.

There is no converter option controlling point merging. The failing determinant metric is a known weak point of boundary-edge tetrahedra in OpenFOAM’s cell-determinant test even when Gmsh reports positive, optimized tetrahedra. I’ll preserve the tetra mesh, then try OpenFOAM’s conformal `polyDualMesh` conversion; dual polyhedra often remove this tetra-specific determinant degeneracy while retaining the exact boundary patches.
I’ll dualize with a 30° feature threshold so the 90° spinner/ring edges and all patch junctions are preserved.

`polyDualMesh` wrote the dual mesh at time `0` rather than replacing `constant/polyMesh`, because diagnostic sets from the prior check created a `0` time. I’ll test that dual mesh first; if it passes, I’ll move its `polyMesh` into `constant` and remove transient diagnostics.

The dual mesh removes the determinant issue but introduces three worse polyhedral quality failures, so I’m discarding it. I’ll switch to a coarse Cartesian cut-cell workflow with `snappyHexMesh`, using the four required STL patches as the closed surface. A 2 mm background grid with level-2 surface refinement gives approximately 0.5 mm cells in each 1 mm gap while avoiding tetrahedral determinant pathology.
The background mesh is 3,456 cells as intended. I’ll now run castellated refinement and snapping against the four exported patch surfaces.

Snappy produced a 45,824-cell predominantly hexahedral mesh with no quality violations under its controls. I’ll now run the full binding topology and geometry checks and inspect patch coverage and mesh volume.

The mesh is closed, one region, correctly patched, and otherwise high quality, but the full checker rejects 432 concave cut cells. I’ll tighten Snappy’s allowable face concavity from 80° to 10° and rerun from the clean background mesh so snapping backs out the deformations that create those cells.
The tightened run completed with zero faces exceeding 10° concavity under Snappy’s quality controls. I’ll run the full checker again.

The stricter snapping removes concave faces but not 432 concave *cells* inherited from the castellated cut-cell topology. I’ll inspect OpenFOAM’s cell-splitting utility; targeted splitting of only the checker-generated `concaveCells` set can make those polyhedra convex without changing the surface.
`splitCells` supports a targeted cell set and geometric cuts. I’ll back up the current snapped mesh, split only `concaveCells` at a 10° edge-angle threshold, and then recheck.
All 432 candidate cells were split in two passes. I’ll run the full checker on the resulting mesh.

Targeted `splitCells` worsened quality, so I’m restoring the pre-split snapped mesh and abandoning that route. I’ll try cfMesh’s Cartesian mesher on a temporary combined multi-solid STL (kept outside `constant/triSurface`, so the four requested patch files remain unchanged). cfMesh preserves STL solid names as patches and usually decomposes boundary cuts more robustly.
I’ll run cfMesh with 2 mm bulk cells and 0.5 mm boundary cells, matching the successful Snappy resolution.
cfMesh completed and reported zero inverted or bad faces after untangling. I’ll now run full checks and verify that all four solid names survived as patches.

cfMesh’s quality is excellent, but it ignored the internal spinner (empty spinner patch and full-cylinder volume \(1.66\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^3}\)), so this mesh is geometrically wrong. The mesh dictionary explicitly disabled “glued mesh” detection; I’ll enable it so cfMesh treats the oppositely oriented internal spinner shell as an obstacle, then rerun.
The glued-surface run found and untangled the internal interface, ending with zero bad faces. I’ll verify volume, spinner coverage, and full mesh quality now.
